subject: Administrative Law
question: Discuss the main grounds on which the court reviews the exercise of discretionary powers by the administration.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Administrative authorities are often given **discretionary powers**: the freedom to choose between different courses of action. But this freedom is not unlimited. Through **judicial review**, courts make sure that the power is used lawfully, reasonably and in good faith.

sections.heading: Grounds of Judicial Review

points.title: Abuse of discretion
points.text: Discretion is abused when the authority uses its power for an **improper purpose**, acts in **bad faith (mala fides)**, or takes **irrelevant considerations** into account while ignoring relevant ones.

points.title: Failure to exercise discretion
points.text: The authority fails to use its discretion when it **acts under dictation** of a superior, **fetters its discretion** with rigid rules, or **delegates** it without authority.

points.title: Unreasonableness
points.text: A decision that is **so unreasonable** that no sensible authority could have taken it can be struck down. This is the **Wednesbury principle**.

points.title: Proportionality
points.text: Where fundamental rights are affected, courts also ask whether the action is **proportionate** to the aim it seeks to achieve.

sections.tip: Write each ground as a **heading**, explain it in two lines, and add **one case** under it.

cases.name: Rohtas Industries v. S.D. Agarwal (1969)
cases.text: The Supreme Court held that even when an authority acts on its **subjective satisfaction**, the court can examine whether the circumstances it relied on were **relevant** to the purpose of the power.

cases.name: Associated Provincial Picture Houses v. Wednesbury Corporation (1948)
cases.text: The English Court of Appeal held that a decision can be struck down if it is **so unreasonable** that no reasonable authority could ever have come to it.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paras: Judicial review keeps discretionary power within the **rule of law**. The authority may choose, but it must choose **fairly**, **reasonably** and for the **right purpose**.

myth.myth: Police can arrest anyone without a warrant.
myth.law: Without a warrant, police can arrest only in **cognizable offences**, and only on the conditions in **Section 35 of the BNSS**.
myth.source_say: Section 35 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, which replaced Section 41 of the CrPC.
myth.thumb: Can police arrest without a warrant?

quiz.question: Which case gave us the **basic structure** doctrine?
quiz.explain: In **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)**, a 13-judge bench held that Parliament cannot change the **basic structure** of the Constitution.

case.name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)
case.facts: Letters to the Supreme Court reported deaths in police custody.
case.issue: What must the police do every time they arrest a person?
case.held: The Court laid down **11 guidelines**: arrest memo, informing a friend or relative, medical check-up, meeting a lawyer, and more.
case.principle: Custodial violence violates **Article 21**. Every arrest must follow the **D.K. Basu guidelines**.

compare.title: Murder: old law vs new law
compare.title_say: Murder. Old law versus new law.

rows.label: Definition
rows.say: Murder was defined in Section 300 of the IPC. It is now Section 101 of the BNS.

rows.label: Punishment
rows.say: Punishment was in Section 302. Now it is Section 103, sub-section 1.

rows.label: Mob lynching
rows.say: And mob lynching, which had no separate offence, is now covered by Section 103, sub-section 2.

steps.title: FIR
steps.say: The FIR is registered under Section 173 of the BNSS.

steps.title: Investigation
steps.say: The police investigate and collect evidence.

steps.title: Police report
steps.say: The police file their report, the chargesheet, under Section 193.

steps.title: Trial & judgment
steps.say: Then comes the trial, and finally the judgment.
